Pool Leak Repair in Phoenix

In a Phoenix summer a pool can drop a lot of water without a single leak. When it drops faster than the heat explains, one free call, any hour, puts you through to an independent, locally owned pool service company.

Call (623) 240-0428 Run the bucket test
  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. Pool Leak Repair

Pool leak repair in Phoenix starts with a question most owners in milder places never have to ask: is this pool actually leaking, or is the desert just drinking it? Valley pools lose a surprising amount of water to the air every summer. A leak hides inside that loss until the numbers stop adding up.

This page shows how to tell the two apart, how to run the bucket test safely, where leaks usually hide, what a leak detection visit involves, and how patches and crack repairs work. It also covers who in Arizona is licensed for which repairs.

Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro does not find or fix leaks. It is a free phone line. Call (623) 240-0428 any hour, an automated assistant asks what the pool is doing, and the call is transferred to an independent, locally owned pool service company. That company hunts down the leak, prices the fix, makes the repair and sends you its own bill.

Evaporation or a leak in a Phoenix summer

Start with what normal looks like. The Arizona Department of Water Resources puts average evaporation in Phoenix at about six feet of water a year, most of it in summer. A City of Mesa chart for a 400 square foot pool adds up to about 79 inches a year, close to 20,000 gallons. A similar table from the City of Scottsdale shows the loss peaking at about 10.8 inches in June, which works out to roughly a third of an inch a day, and falling to about 2.6 inches in January.

So a pool that drops a quarter or a third of an inch on a hot, dry, breezy June day may be perfectly sound. Water features, a spa spillover, heavy splashing and wind all add to the loss. What should get your attention is a drop that is clearly bigger than the season explains, a drop that continues in winter when evaporation is low, or a pool that loses more when the pump is running than when it is off.

Leaks are not rare. The City of Mesa estimates that up to 30 percent of pools may have a leak. An autofill can hide one for months, with the only clue a higher water bill, which is one more reason to check the meter or the bill against last year's.

The bucket test, step by step

This is the standard way to separate evaporation from a leak, and it needs nothing more than a bucket and a marker. The bucket and the pool sit in the same sun and wind, so they should lose about the same amount to evaporation.

  1. Turn off the autofill if the pool has one, so it cannot top the pool up during the test.
  2. Fill a bucket with pool water and set it on the first or second step, so the bucket's water level is close to the pool's.
  3. Mark both levels. Mark the water line inside the bucket, and mark the pool's level on the tile or skimmer with tape or a grease pencil.
  4. Run the pump on its normal schedule and leave everything alone for two to three days. Calm, dry days give the cleanest result; rain or strong wind can throw it off.
  5. Compare the drops. If the pool fell noticeably more than the bucket, the pool is losing water some other way.
  6. Optional second round: repeat with the pump off. A bigger loss with the pump running points toward the pressure side plumbing; a loss that continues with the pump off points toward the shell, fittings or suction lines.

Keep children away from the pool while you work around it, and never leave a child alone near the water. Do not climb in to inspect anything while the pump is running.

Where pool leaks hide

Most leaks show up at the places where something passes through the pool shell or where two materials meet. Water can also leave from plumbing under the deck or from the equipment pad. Use this table to describe what you see when you call.

Common pool leak locations, the clues they leave, and typical repairs
WhereClues you might seeTypical repair
Skimmer throatWater stops dropping at the bottom of the skimmer opening; a crack or gap where the skimmer meets the tile or shellUnderwater putty or sealant at the joint, or skimmer repair or replacement for a cracked body
Light nicheWater stops dropping at the light; a gap around the conduit at the back of the nicheSealing the conduit and niche with a pool rated sealant. The light's wiring is electrical work
Return and other fittingsDye pulls toward a return, cleaner line, drain or step jetSealing or replacing the fitting and patching the plaster around it
Underground plumbingBigger loss with the pump running, wet or sinking deck spots, air in the pump basket, cracks in the deckPressure testing each line, then digging or cutting the deck to repair the broken section
Equipment padDrips or puddles at the pump, filter, valves or heater, or water from the backwash line when it should be closedReplacing o-rings, unions, seals or valves, often a smaller fix
Cracks in the shellA visible crack in the floor, walls or the tile line, sometimes with dye drawn into itPatching for minor cracks; for structural cracks, finding out why the shell moved before repairing it
  • Note where the water stops. If the level falls and then holds at a certain height, the leak is often at or near that height, such as the skimmer or the light.
  • Walk the equipment pad and look for drips, wet dirt or puddles, without opening anything.
  • Look at the deck for new cracks, damp patches or spots that have settled.
  • Check the pump basket lid for air bubbles, which can mean a suction side leak.

What pool leak detection involves

Leak detection is a process of narrowing things down. A careful pool technician usually works from the simplest checks to the more involved ones.

  1. Confirm the loss. Review the bucket test, the water bill or the autofill, and how the level behaves with the pump on and off.
  2. Look over the equipment and deck. Many leaks turn out to be at the pad.
  3. Dye testing. With the water still, a small amount of test dye is released next to fittings, cracks and the skimmer. If the dye is pulled into a gap, water is leaving there. This often means the technician gets in the pool.
  4. Pressure testing. Each plumbing line is plugged and pressurized. A line that will not hold pressure is leaking somewhere along its length.
  5. Listening equipment. Sensitive microphones on the deck or in the water help pinpoint where a pressurized line is leaking underground, so less deck has to be opened.

Ask for a written summary of what was tested and what was found. If a line has to be dug up, ask how much deck will be cut and how it will be patched.

Patching a pool: what works with the water in

Small leaks in the shell or around fittings are often fixed without draining. Pool professionals use epoxy putties and patching compounds made to cure underwater. The material is pressed into a clean, sound spot and shaped. It is quick and keeps the pool full, which matters in a city that asks residents to drain pools only rarely.

Good candidates for an underwater patch

  • A small crack or chip that dye shows is leaking
  • A gap between a fitting and the plaster
  • The joint where the skimmer meets the shell
  • A small hole or tear in a vinyl liner, with a vinyl patch

When a patch is not enough

  • Plaster that is soft, hollow or flaking over a wide area
  • A crack that keeps growing or runs through the shell
  • A leak in buried plumbing
  • Several leaks across an old, worn surface

When the surface itself is worn out, the answer may be replastering or another new interior rather than one more patch. Our pool resurfacing page explains those options, and the guide on whether to repair or resurface a pool helps you weigh the cost of patches against a new surface.

Can a cracked pool be repaired?

Most cracked pools can be repaired. The question is what kind of crack it is. Fine, shallow cracks in the plaster, sometimes called check cracks or crazing, are common in older surfaces and are mostly cosmetic. A crack that leaks, widens, shows a step from one side to the other, or runs through the tile line and bond beam may mean the shell has moved. That needs a diagnosis of the cause, such as soil movement or a plumbing leak washing out the ground underneath, before a lasting repair is chosen.

Licensing for leak, plumbing and crack repair in Arizona

Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) licenses contractors, and the classification matters for leak work. The ROC's R-6 Swimming Pool Service and Repair classification covers servicing pools and minor repairs, but it lists plumbing connections to a drinking water system, gas lines and electrical work beyond the first disconnect as outside its scope, and it does not allow a complete replacement of a plaster or pebble interior or the deck. So a pool company may patch a fitting under its R-6 license, while larger shell, plumbing or replastering work may call for a different classification. Ask the company which license covers the work it is quoting, then confirm it on the ROC contractor search.

Questions worth asking before the leak work starts

  • How will you find the leak, and is detection priced separately from the repair?
  • What did the dye and pressure tests show, and can I see it?
  • Is this crack cosmetic or structural, and how do you know?
  • Can it be patched with the water in, or does the level need to come down?
  • If water must be removed, where will it go?
  • What is your ROC license number and classification?

Common questions

How do I know if my pool is leaking or just evaporating?

Use the bucket test. Set a bucket of pool water on a step so its water level matches the pool's, mark both levels, and compare after two or three days with the autofill off. If the pool drops noticeably more than the bucket, water is going somewhere besides the air. The City of Scottsdale describes this test and notes that rain and wind can skew the result, so try it on calm, dry days.

Can you patch a pool with water in it?

Often, yes, for small problems. Pool professionals use putties and patching compounds made to cure underwater for small cracks, chips and gaps around fittings such as the skimmer or a light. The pool stays full, so swimming and water balance are barely affected. Bigger cracks, large areas of failing plaster or anything structural usually need the water lowered or the pool drained, and that is a bigger job with its own rules about where the water goes.

How do you patch a pool?

First the leak has to be found exactly, often with a few drops of test dye near a suspected spot. The area is cleaned of loose material, and a patching product rated for pools, and for underwater use if the pool is full, is pressed in and shaped according to its label. On vinyl liners, a patch made for vinyl is used. Patching a pinpoint spot you can clearly see is a reasonable homeowner task with a product made for it; a leak you cannot find, or one in plumbing, is a job for a pool company.

Can a cracked pool be repaired?

Usually. Fine surface cracks in plaster are common and are often patched or handled at the next resurfacing. Cracks that leak, grow or run through the shell or the bond beam under the tile are different: they need someone to work out why the shell is moving before choosing a repair. Ask the company to explain whether a crack is cosmetic or structural, and check its Arizona ROC license before any structural work.

Who finds pool leaks in the Phoenix area?

Many pool service and repair companies do leak detection, using dye, pressure tests on the plumbing and listening equipment. Call the line, say how much water the pool is losing and what you have already checked, and you are put through to a local pool company. Ask for its ROC license number and look it up before any repair work starts.
